name: Erik Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 43, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, still learning the trade after leaving warehouse administration. My employer pays above the usual rate, but I still need help with fault diagnosis and a senior checks and signs off my work. My partner Nadia is a technical writer, our children are eight and fifteen, and we've a mortgage and a year's expenses saved, with plenty of electrical employers nearby. I use AI every day to make myself short study quizzes, checking the answers against my course book; I love trying things, though my hands are often slower than my enthusiasm and I hate letting the crew down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small useful study tool is still worth having when the big promises shrink. I'd like the saved office time used to explain jobs properly to juniors. We don't need a revolution to make a working week a bit fairer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the mortgage and bills comfortably enough, and the year's reserve makes learning this trade an affordable choice. Nadia's writing work carries on much as before in this picture. I feel secure, not cheated because the software stops short of the big promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing supervised electrical shifts through the next year. This month I'd buy an 80 educational low-voltage practice board from my separate hobby budget and use it to rehearse course exercises, with my senior checking my understanding in normal shifts. I'd continue the daily checked AI quizzes, never treat them as permission to work unsupervised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite excited about getting my hands to catch up with my head. I can enjoy being a beginner when the house isn't resting on next week's quiz score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use that practice board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise on the little educational board without connecting anything to a home installation. Then I'd take a photograph of the exercise and ask the senior what I'd misunderstood. A neat practice board wouldn't mean I could sign off somebody's wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the children one thing I got wrong and how I corrected it. My younger child likes catching me out on the quiz. I want learning to look like ordinary effort, not something adults pretend they've finished.

say: I'd value a **small study tool** even if the biggest AI promises shrink.
I'd ask for saved time to support **fairer junior learning**, without needing a revolution first.
think: Our wages and **year's reserve** make the mortgage and my career change feel secure.
Nadia's **writing income** carries on much as before in this modest-change picture.
do: Keep **supervised electrical shifts** and daily checked study quizzes through the next year.
Buy an **80 practice board** this month from the separate hobby budget for educational exercises.
feel: **Calm and curious**, able to enjoy beginner status without immediate pressure on the household.
S0.quote: A neat practice board wouldn't mean I could sign off somebody's wiring.
fieldNote: His **strong finances** support genuine baseline calm while high pay never changes his junior electrical competence.
The **educational board** is separate from home installations, and both quizzes and practice remain subject to senior checking.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical work and checked daily study quizzes
Buy the 80 educational practice board from the separate hobby budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team thinking tasks include Nadia's paid writing, not just our quotations. I'd ask the workers' association to seek paid learning for junior and office staff before faster software becomes a reason to cut hours. My enthusiasm for a tool isn't permission to make somebody else carry the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own junior hours could shrink if estimating savings turn into tighter crews. Nadia's technical writing looks more exposed now, and her projects could get smaller or fewer. Our reserve gives us control over the first shock, but I can't call the household income safe just because I hold a cable for part of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take a proposal for paid junior learning to the association, asking colleagues to add what they need. In the first year I'd learn the approved AI drawing-explanation tool alongside my senior and check it against ten course drawings before using it for study. Nadia and I would also stop the 100 monthly holiday contribution and redirect it into the emergency account while both wages covered bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for the household, and still interested in what the tools can teach me. Those feelings don't cancel each other. I don't want to learn quickly by looking away from the work my partner might lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you discuss with your partner first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nadia which paid tasks had actually changed and whether the hours in the next contract were confirmed. I wouldn't give my partner a lecture about being more adaptable. A cheaper piece of software can change a skilled person's market without making that person lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the drawing-explanation tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the explanation against the course drawing and ask the senior where it was misleading. If the answer sounded confident but was wrong, I'd keep that example for the tool review. A fluent explanation isn't an electrical test.

say: I'd include **paid writing** in the discussion instead of focusing only on electrical quotations.
I'd seek **paid learning** through the association before savings become pressure on workers' hours.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink, while Nadia's writing projects face more immediate thinking-AI pressure.
The reserve gives us **some control**, but neither cable work nor enthusiasm guarantees household income.
do: Propose **paid junior learning** through the association with colleagues' input.
Learn the **drawing-explanation tool** with ten course drawings checked by the senior.
Redirect **100 monthly** from holiday contributions into emergency savings while essentials stay covered.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, unwilling to let his own enthusiasm hide risks to his partner's paid work.
S1.quote: A fluent explanation isn't an electrical test.
fieldNote: His **household exposure** includes technical writing as well as possible junior-hours pressure, despite plentiful local electrical employers.
The **tool trial** is for checked study, and the new emergency transfer comes from a real discretionary contribution.

steps.text: Seek paid junior learning through the workers’ association
Learn the drawing-explanation tool with ten supervised course examples
Redirect 100 monthly from holiday contributions into emergency savings while bills remain covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work our household faces 2028 before a robot touches my fitting tasks. Nadia's technical writing is thinking work; capable robots come around 2031 for the physical jobs. I'd ask for honest notice and paid transition options, not call electrical work a family escape hatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Nadia's writing income to go when thinking AGI arrives. My wage is good for this job but doesn't cover our present mortgage and all family costs on its own, and my junior hours could later shrink too. A year's reserve is a long buffer, not a permanent second wage. I'd lose sleep over how to replace the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd redirect the holiday 100 into emergency savings and book a fee-free household advice appointment to check essential spending and mortgage options without assuming relief. In 2029 I'd enrol in a short supervised electrical fault-diagnosis course from a separate study budget, keeping all basic shifts and the year's reserve intact. I'd also help the association seek paid transition training, without treating an unagreed proposal as a funded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even though I'm not out of ideas. I can imagine spending carefully through the reserve while Nadia's former work doesn't return. I don't want to confuse being excited by technology with being ready to lose a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the adviser to examine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring both wage histories, our actual essential bills and the mortgage terms. I'd ask what could be changed before a missed payment, not assume a lender would agree or a public payment would arrive. We need the costed choices before we make promises to the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether the course improved your position?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I could diagnose more faults correctly under supervision, then look at actual vacancies before imagining a better wage. It wouldn't make me a licensed electrician or make fault work safe from later robots. The course is an experiment I can afford, not a replacement income I already have.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 writing income** from capable robots reaching physical work around 2031.
I'd seek **honest notice** and paid transition options rather than call electrical work a guaranteed household escape.
think: I expect **most writing income** to disappear, while my wage alone doesn't cover our present family costs.
A **year's reserve** buffers the gap without permanently replacing a second wage or protecting later junior hours.
do: Redirect **100 monthly** into emergency savings and obtain fee-free household advice now.
Enrol in **2029 fault-diagnosis study** from the separate budget, keeping every basic shift and emergency savings intact.
Seek **paid transition training** through the association without assuming an agreed funded place.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting a major household loss while retaining affordable experiments and advice to pursue.
S2.quote: A year's reserve is a long buffer, not a permanent second wage.
fieldNote: Alarm follows expected **household earnings loss** at the thinking-AI date rather than incorrect early robotic replacement.
Study preserves **basic shifts and reserves**, while the adviser checks actual terms and no lender relief or public support is presumed.

steps.text: Redirect the 100 holiday contribution monthly into emergency savings
Get fee-free household advice on actual spending and mortgage options
Take fault-diagnosis study in 2029 from separate funds with all shifts retained
Seek paid transition training through the workers’ association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to reduce the household's dependence on a wage that looks exposed. That doesn't mean the writing income is protected. Thinking AGI comes in 2031 and capable robots around 2034, so we'd need to use the first years instead of celebrating the delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a big loss to Nadia's writing income in 2031, and that worries me enough to wake at night. More time could let us change costs and test what I can do, but it doesn't guarantee my junior electrical wage grows enough. I'd rather admit the missing income than call our savings a solution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in the short supervised fault-diagnosis course from the separate study budget, retaining all basic shifts. We'd use fee-free advice this year to make a costed household plan and redirect the monthly holiday 100 into emergency savings. In 2032 I'd apply for actual paid supervised maintenance vacancies only if written hours, travel and pay improved our essential budget; the association's paid-training proposal would continue alongside that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected wage loss, but less hurried about each decision. I can test one course before buying another. I can't put a certificate into the mortgage account and call it earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you assume about your partner finding other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia would list what work actually paid and check genuine offers outside writing if interested, without us counting an income before the terms existed. I'd support that without announcing a safe new occupation on my partner's behalf. The household plan has to show unknowns as unknowns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop the course becoming false reassurance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the tutor to show me what I still couldn't do safely and compare that with vacancy duties. A better test result is useful, but it isn't proof of a bigger wage. I'd keep my present job until an acceptable written offer actually existed.

I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AGI** from later capable robots around 2034 when planning household changes.
think: I still expect a **large writing-income loss**, with no guarantee that my junior wage can replace it.
More time lets us test costs and skills, but **savings aren't earnings** and the gap remains worrying.
do: Take the **fault-diagnosis course** now from separate funds with every basic shift retained.
Obtain **fee-free budget advice** and redirect the holiday 100 into emergency savings.
Seek **2032 supervised vacancies** only on written terms improving our essential budget, while pursuing association training terms.
feel: **Alarmed with more time**, able to check decisions carefully without mistaking a certificate for replacement earnings.
S3.quote: I can't put a certificate into the mortgage account and call it earnings.
fieldNote: The expected **household income loss** remains large despite a stronger buffer and extra preparation years, supporting continued alarm.
His partner's **replacement income** stays unknown, and any job change requires real supervised work and acceptable written pay and travel terms.

steps.text: Take supervised fault-diagnosis study from separate funds while retaining basic shifts
Use fee-free household advice to cost the income gap
Save the 100 monthly holiday contribution for emergencies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team ten years lets us make learning part of the paid week instead of a household emergency. I'd keep pushing that through the association. I don't want people told to spend a decade buying courses while employers keep every minute the machines save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own wages and living costs feel secure over the next few years, with time to test smaller changes before 2036. I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives, still needing income when robots follow around 2039. The later writing-income problem matters, but I don't assume our household will still have exactly today's costs and options in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the short supervised course now from the separate study budget and keep my basic shifts. We'd redirect the holiday 100 for a year, then review real costs, both wages and actual vacancies annually before committing to more study. In 2037 I'd apply for suitable paid supervised maintenance work only on written terms improving our essential budget, while helping the association pursue paid transition training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later income question, but secure enough now to enjoy learning rather than race it. I could watch the children grow without treating every family purchase as the last one we'll afford. I'd still want the annual review written in the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual review measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual paid hours from both jobs, emergency savings measured against real costs, and what duties vacancies offered. If the wages weakened earlier, we'd bring advice and applications forward. An annual plan isn't permission to ignore an earlier payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop enthusiasm taking over the family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd agree the study budget with Nadia before spending it, including a limit for any extra course. Enthusiasm can be expensive if I let every new tool become essential. I'd keep at least two evenings a week free of courses and screens for the family.

I'd ask the **association** to negotiate a share of saved time for the workers learning new tasks.
think: Our **near-term wages** and living costs feel secure, leaving time to test smaller changes.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need future income, while household costs and options may change before then.

Save the holiday **100 monthly** for one year before reviewing actual costs and wages.
Seek suitable **2037 supervised work** on better written budget terms, while pursuing paid transition training through the association.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, able to enjoy family life and learning while keeping a real annual review.
S4.quote: An annual plan isn't permission to ignore an earlier payslip.
fieldNote: His mood changes because **near-term household security** remains intact and later costs and options are not assumed fixed for a decade.
Study has an agreed **separate budget**, basic shifts remain protected, and any later application depends on real written affordability.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect Nadia's writing income to fall before we've tested a different household plan. Early notice, paid transition learning and honest advice using our actual mortgage would help; any new job needs real paid hours, not just a promising title. Our family reserve can buy time, but the mortgage keeps spending that time with us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether liking AI makes it awkward to admit the household could lose from it. It does sometimes, but I don't owe a machine a cheerful answer. I can be curious and still ask for the people doing the work to have a say.

headlineQuote: Our family reserve can buy time, but the mortgage keeps spending that time with us.
portrait: At **43**, Erik is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, higher pay, and a full year of household expenses saved.
He and **Nadia**, his technical-writer partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with plentiful nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI daily** for checked quizzes and affordable experiments, while recognising that electrical competence still requires supervision and senior sign-off.
His **progressive outlook** supports shared transition terms; expected writing-income losses can cause alarm despite strong savings and enthusiasm for the tools.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove much of his partner's writing income before a different household plan has been tested.
whatWouldHelp: **Early notice**, paid transition learning and advice based on the actual mortgage would help, with real paid hours for any replacement job.
